beats.vo: But salt only stops the shortcut. It doesn't stop guessing.
An attacker with a leaked salt and hash can still try passwords one by one. Hash a guess with that salt, compare, repeat.

lines.text: nearly half: names, words, slang, patterns
likely guesses first, the long tail later
and these hashes are fast to calculate

beats.vo: Real people make that easier. In the Rock You leak, nearly half the passwords were names, dictionary words or simple patterns.
So attackers try the likely passwords first, and the long tail later.
And the hashes we've seen so far are fast to calculate.
Take one gaming graphics card, an R T X forty ninety, running the cracking tool hash cat.
It tries about a hundred and sixty-four billion M D five guesses every second.
About fifty billion for SHA one. About twenty-two billion for SHA two fifty-six.

props.title: one RTX 4090 running hashcat
props.note: each card stands for over a billion guesses · hashcat benchmark

props.title: every 8-character password of a–z and 0–9 · 2.8 trillion · full-search estimate

beats.vo: Take every possible eight-character password made of lowercase letters and digits. That's about two point eight trillion of them.
With M D five, that card gets through all of them in about seventeen seconds. With SHA one, under a minute. SHA two fifty-six, about two minutes.

lines.text: slow on purpose · tunable as hardware improves

beats.vo: So the real fix is to make each guess expensive.
Password hashing functions are built to be slow on purpose, and the slowness can be turned up as hardware gets faster.
B crypt arrived in nineteen ninety-nine.

props.title: same RTX 4090 · slow hashes
props.note: drawn far from scale: bcrypt here is about 900,000× slower than MD5

beats.vo: On the same card, B crypt at a low setting manages about a hundred and eighty-four thousand guesses a second. That same set of passwords now takes about half a year.
S crypt arrived in two thousand nine. It also makes each guess use a lot of memory, to blunt custom cracking hardware.
At the tested setting, the card manages about seven thousand guesses a second. About twelve and a half years for the same set.

lines.text: OWASP recommends · from Argon2, competition winner 2015

beats.vo: The Oh wasp guidance on password storage recommends Argon two I D. It comes from Argon two, which won an open password hashing competition in twenty fifteen.
Its minimum setting uses about twenty megabytes of memory and two rounds of work for every single guess.

props.title: what the database stores for you
props.caption: Settings travel with the hash, so the cost can be raised later

beats.vo: In a common library's format, the stored value carries its own recipe. One line holds the algorithm and its settings. Then the salt. Then the hash.
Because the settings travel with the hash, a site can raise the cost later. It re-hashes your password the next time you log in.

lines.text: one secret, kept outside the database

beats.vo: Some sites add one more layer, called a pepper. It's a single secret kept outside the database, so a stolen table alone isn't enough to start guessing.

lines.text: a salt and a slow fingerprint per row

beats.vo: So picture the grocery app's table leaking today. Each row gives an attacker a salt and a slow fingerprint, and every guess costs real time.
